children: From Jan Dhan and JAM to bank consolidation, bad-loan clean-up and UPI, India’s banking sector has undergone a structural transformation since 2014

As Prime Minister Narendra Modi turns 76, India’s banking sector stands markedly different from the one his government inherited in 2014. The transformation has unfolded across three broad fronts: financial inclusion, the clean-up and consolidation of banks, and a rapid shift towards digital banking.

One of the earliest pillars was the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, launched in August 2014 to bring people outside the formal financial system into banking. By August 2026, more than 59 crore Jan-Dhan accounts had been opened, with deposits of about Rs 3.17 lakh crore. Around 56 per cent of the accounts were held by women and 78 per cent were in rural and semi-urban areas.

The importance of Jan Dhan has extended beyond opening bank accounts. Combined with Aadhaar and mobile connectivity, the JAM framework has become a major channel for direct benefit transfers. The government says Rs 6.9 lakh crore was credited through various DBT schemes during 2024-25.

The other major change has been the restructuring of public sector banking. The government consolidated several state-owned banks, including the merger of Vijaya Bank and Dena Bank with Bank of Baroda in 2019.

In 2020, another 10 public sector banks were merged into four entities: Punjab National Bank, Canara Bank, Union Bank of India and Indian Bank. The stated objective was to create larger institutions with greater scale, technology capabilities and capacity to support a growing economy.

At the same time, the banking system underwent a prolonged clean-up of stressed assets. The RBI’s 2015 Asset Quality Review exposed the extent of bad loans, followed by measures involving recognition, resolution, recovery and recapitalisation. According to the Economic Survey 2025-26, the gross NPA ratio of scheduled commercial banks had fallen to a multi-decadal low, while the capital adequacy ratio stood at 17.2 per cent in September 2025.

Digitalisation has arguably been the most visible change for ordinary customers. UPI, mobile banking, digital lending and Account Aggregator infrastructure have altered how Indians make payments and access financial services. Public sector banks are now also deploying data-based underwriting, GST information and bank-statement integration in lending processes.

Yet the transformation has not eliminated the sector’s challenges. Cyber fraud, customer protection, digital exclusion, stressed borrowers and the need for stronger governance remain concerns. The next phase will involve balancing rapid credit expansion with prudent lending and ensuring that technology expands access without creating new vulnerabilities.

For Modi’s 76th birthday, India’s banking story is therefore less about a single reform than about a structural shift, from a branch-and-cash dominated system towards one that is broader, more consolidated and increasingly digital.
